title: Asking for a Favor Makes Them Like You
text:
In his autobiography, Benjamin Franklin describes how he won over a hostile fellow legislator. Instead of flattering him, Franklin asked to borrow a rare book from the man's library. The rival lent it, Franklin returned it with a warm note of thanks, and from then on the man treated him with civility and later friendship. Franklin concluded that someone who has done you a kindness is more ready to do you another than someone you have helped.

In 1969 the psychologists Jon Jecker and David Landy put the idea to a test. Students took part in a task in which they won some money from the experimenter. Afterward, one group was approached by the experimenter himself, who explained that he was paying out of his own pocket, was running short, and asked if they would mind giving the money back. A second group was asked by a departmental secretary to return it to the psychology department's research fund. A third group kept the money.

Then everyone rated how much they liked the experimenter. Those who had done him a personal favor liked him the most, more than those who had kept their winnings. Doing someone a kindness, it seemed, led people to justify it by liking that person more.
lesson: Letting people help you can build a relationship faster than helping them. A modest, sincere request for advice or a small favor is an invitation, not a burden.
source: Jecker, J., and Landy, D. (1969). Liking a person as a function of doing him a favor. Human Relations, 22(4), 371-378.
caveat: The original experiment was small, so the size of the effect should be taken with some caution.
